props.title: Crimes and Misdemeanors

sections.content: Crimes and Misdemeanors (1989) represents Woody Allen at his most philosophically complex, weaving together two storylines that explore morality, justice, and the existence of God. The film's primary narrative follows successful ophthalmologist Judah Rosenthal (Martin Landau) arranging the murder of his mistress to protect his reputation, while a parallel story tracks Allen's documentary filmmaker character pursuing an unfulfilling project about a pompous TV producer (Alan Alda). The film's brilliant interweaving of comedy and existential drama echoes Ingmar Bergman's The Seventh Seal (1957) and Federico Fellini's 8½ (1963) in its exploration of faith, guilt, and ethical choices.

sections.content: The film's mastery lies in how it uses the two contrasting storylines to examine moral relativism. While Judah grapples with murder and its aftermath, Allen's character Cliff deals with comparatively trivial ethical compromises in his work. This parallel structure recalls Alfred Hitchcock's Strangers on a Train (1951) and Michael Powell's Peeping Tom (1960) in showing how ordinary people can rationalize increasingly disturbing behavior. The film's use of Rabbi Ben, who's going blind, serves as a powerful metaphor for moral blindness.

Allen's direction demonstrates remarkable restraint, letting scenes breathe in ways that recall Bergman's Winter Light (1963). The murder sequence is handled entirely off-screen, focusing instead on Judah's psychological torture. This approach stands in stark contrast to later moral thrillers like A Simple Plan (1998) or Before the Devil Knows You're Dead (2007), which emphasize the visceral aspects of crime. Instead, Allen keeps the focus squarely on the philosophical implications of getting away with murder. SUBHEAD: Religious and Philosophical Themes

sections.content: The film's Jewish religious elements provide a crucial framework for its moral questioning. Judah's memories of Passover seders and discussions of the eyes of God watching humanity create a theological dimension that elevates the film beyond simple crime drama. This religious wrestling with conscience recalls Robert Bresson's Diary of a Country Priest (1951) and Carl Theodor Dreyer's Ordet (1955) in its serious treatment of faith in crisis.
